items.label: f02-isvalidemail-too-loose
items.front: Both lesson tests pass, yet `isValidEmail("@.")` returns what — and what does that say about the two tests?
items.back: true: it only checks that "@" and "." appear somewhere. Two happy/sad examples did not pin down the rule; add edge cases (missing local part, dot before @).

items.label: f04-parseuser-conflates-failures
items.front: A caller of `parseUser` gets null. Can it tell whether the input was broken JSON or a user without a name?
items.back: No: both failures go through one catch and return null; only the console log differs. Return a result with a reason, or throw distinct errors, when callers must react differently.

items.label: f03-innerhtml-from-api
items.front:
`loadPosts` renders with `list.innerHTML = posts.map(post => `
  • ${post.title}
    • `)`. A post title contains ``. What happens?
items.back: The markup is parsed and the handler runs (XSS). Build elements and set textContent for API data, or escape it, instead of interpolating into innerHTML.

items.label: f01-date-now-id-collision
items.front: The tasks API assigns `id: Date.now()`. Two POSTs land within the same millisecond. What breaks later?
items.back: Both tasks get the same id, so a DELETE or PATCH by id (Labs 07A/07B) hits the wrong task or both. Use a counter, crypto.randomUUID(), or a database key.

items.prompt: Why does `wait(ms)` build `new Promise(resolve => setTimeout(resolve, ms))` instead of just returning `setTimeout(...)`?

choices.text: Without the wrapper the timer fires immediately, because ms would be ignored
The wrapper runs the delay on a separate thread so it cannot block rendering
setTimeout already returns a promise, and wrapping it only adds proper error handling
setTimeout returns a timer id, which cannot be awaited, so the wrapper makes a promise

choices: Without the wrapper the timer fires immediately, because ms would be ignored
The wrapper runs the delay on a separate thread so it cannot block rendering
setTimeout already returns a promise, and wrapping it only adds proper error handling
setTimeout returns a timer id, which cannot be awaited, so the wrapper makes a promise

items.explanation: The lesson presents it as the promise version of a delay: handing resolve to the timer gives callers a promise that settles when the delay ends, so `.then` / `await` can wait on it.

items.prompt: Why is `import { double } from "./math.js"` better than defining `double` as a global that app.js just uses?

choices.text: Imported functions run faster, because modules are compiled ahead of time
Globals are unreachable across files, so an import is the one way to share code
The dependency is named in app.js, and math.js's unexported code stays private
import copies the function, so later edits to math.js cannot affect app.js

choices: Imported functions run faster, because modules are compiled ahead of time
Globals are unreachable across files, so an import is the one way to share code
The dependency is named in app.js, and math.js's unexported code stays private
import copies the function, so later edits to math.js cannot affect app.js

items.explanation: Modules reduce hidden global state and make reuse explicit (the lesson's line under the example): the import names the dependency at the top of app.js, and anything math.js does not export stays out of shared global scope.

items.prompt: Why does `loadPosts` test `response.ok` itself instead of trusting its catch block to see failed requests?

choices.text: The check makes fetch retry the request once before the catch block runs
fetch rejects just on a network failure, and a 404 or 500 response still resolves
await throws for 4xx statuses but not 5xx, so the check covers server errors
response.json() would hang on an error status unless ok is checked first

choices: The check makes fetch retry the request once before the catch block runs
fetch rejects just on a network failure, and a 404 or 500 response still resolves
await throws for 4xx statuses but not 5xx, so the check covers server errors
response.json() would hang on an error status unless ok is checked first

items.explanation: The lesson calls this a common beginner mistake: assuming fetch throws on every failed HTTP status. Without the explicit throw on !response.ok the error path would never run.

The task appears twice in the list, once from each instance's copy of it
The list may hit the other instance, whose own array did not see the task

Nothing: both instances share the array, since module variables are host-global
The task appears twice in the list, once from each instance's copy of it
The list may hit the other instance, whose own array did not see the task

items.explanation: The lesson lists the limits of an in-memory array: lost on restart, does not scale across multiple instances. Each instance has its own separate array.

choices.text: Re-run the original reproduction path, as a vanished symptom is not proof
Add a comment explaining the fix, which stands in for re-testing the change
Revert the change and try a different one, to confirm it was not just luck
Change the surrounding layers as well, so the same class of bug cannot recur

items.explanation: Steps 5 and 6: fix one thing at a time, then re-test the original reproduction path. The symptom vanishing does not show the reported behavior is now correct.

items.prompt: A button handler runs `loadPosts(); console.log("after");` without awaiting. When does "after" print relative to the posts appearing?

choices.text: After the posts render, because await inside loadPosts blocks the whole program
Never, since an un-awaited async call cancels the rest of the handler
Before them, because await suspends only loadPosts, not the calling handler
After the posts render, since console output waits for pending fetches

Never, since an un-awaited async call cancels the rest of the handler
Before them, because await suspends only loadPosts, not the calling handler
After the posts render, since console output waits for pending fetches

items.explanation: The lesson: `await` pauses only inside the current async function, not the entire program, so the handler continues as soon as loadPosts hits its first await.

None until called: each instance compiles its own methods lazily on first use
One: class methods live on Cart.prototype and are shared by every instance

items.explanation: The lesson: methods like addItem and getTotal are shared through the class prototype rather than recreated on every instance, and each instance reaches them through the prototype chain; classes are syntactic sugar over prototypes. (Only `this.items` is per instance.)

items.prompt: The Lab 03C `safeParse(json, fallback)` is used for a settings file. What does it give up compared with the lesson's `parseUser`?

choices.text: Nothing, as the optional catch binding still logs every caught error automatically
It cannot parse arrays, because the fallback parameter defaults to null instead
It rethrows parse errors to the caller, which makes it less safe than parseUser
Any trace of the failure, so a corrupt file looks the same as a real fallback value

choices: Nothing, as the optional catch binding still logs every caught error automatically
It cannot parse arrays, because the fallback parameter defaults to null instead
It rethrows parse errors to the caller, which makes it less safe than parseUser
Any trace of the failure, so a corrupt file looks the same as a real fallback value

items.explanation: `catch { return fallback; }` swallows the error entirely - it neither logs nor validates - so a corrupt file and a file that genuinely holds the fallback value look identical. parseUser at least logs `error.message` and checks required data.

items.explanation: The lesson's order is parse, validate, apply logic, store, respond; `return` is what stops invalid input from reaching the store. Without it the handler keeps going after the 400.

items.explanation: The solution only shows the class shape; `this.balance -= amount` has no guard, so the class enforces no business rule against overdrawing (or negative amounts). A real account would validate before mutating.

choices.text: "Error: Status: 503", as any rejected loadUsers lands in showUsers' catch
"Loaded users.", because loadUsers has no try/catch of its own and cannot fail
